english.html: Duke Charles that the people constantly affirmed that the Duke was not dead, and that this man was truly Duke Charles, although he himself affirmed the contrary and stoutly denied that he was <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>. Francesco Sforza, Duke of Milan, had in his service a young soldier who resembled him so well that all the other soldiers, taking their cue from this likeness, often called the young man the Prince; in whom, as in a mirror, the Duke often delighted to see his own image, his gestures and bearing, to recognise his voice, and to contemplate himself. At the same time and in the same country this Duke Sforza had a jester named Marchesino, whom he called the lord Sigismondo Malatesta, his son, because they were entirely alike; at which this Malatesta was so much ashamed that when he wished to go to Milan to see the Duke, his father-in-law, he first sent to beg him to send Marchesino elsewhere. <sup class="mk" data-key="h">h</sup> Of the likenesses that have been the cause of several impostures, great factions and memorable enterprises, we shall speak more conveniently below in some place, if it please the Lord. But here perhaps someone will wish to search out and understand the cause why one often sees men begotten of different parents, and in different and distant places, nevertheless resemble one another so well and so exactly in the features of the face and the composition of the body that they cannot easily be distinguished from one another. To whom I shall say first that one must, with the honour and reverence that are due, refer the source and cause of such facts to the understanding of that great workman of nature (who is God almighty), who is not bound to races, nor to countries, nor to the affections of persons, but by his infinite and incomprehensible providence, and his secret, high and inscrutable judgments, projects his ideas and forms his creatures as seems good to him. Nevertheless one sees it come about most often that the likenesses of men pass down through their races, and that every animal not only begets its like, but also imparts to it its own proper and natural virtues.

notes.citation: Sebastian Münster, Cosmographia universalis, book II (chapter not located)
notes.original: Mũſter au liure ij. de la coſmographie vniuerſelle,
notes.gloss: Charles the Bold was killed at Nancy, 5 January 1477. Coras's Bruxelles "in the diocese of Speyer" is Münster's Bruchsal (Latin Bruxella), not Brussels.

notes.citation: Battista Fregoso (Baptista Fulgosus, 1453–1504), De dictis factisque memorabilibus collectanea IX, c. 15 (as cited; chapter unverified)
notes.original: Raphael fu goſe au liure ix, des choſes memorables c. xv.
notes.gloss: Coras's "Raphael" is a slip for Baptista. Sigismondo Malatesta, lord of Rimini, was Francesco Sforza's son-in-law (he married Polissena Sforza in 1442): Coras first calls him "his son" and then, correctly, has the Duke as his "father-in-law".
Evidently belongs to "Of the likenesses that have been the cause of several impostures … we shall speak more conveniently below," where the print set no marker.

lines: Duc Charles, que le peuple conſtamment aſſeuroit que
le Duc n'eſtoit point mort, & que celuy la eſtoit verita-
blement le Duc Charles, combien que luy-meſme affer
maſt le contraire, & viuement niaſt qu'il le fuſt {g}. Fran-
çois Sforce Duc de Milan, auoit à ſon ſeruice vn ieune
ſoldat, qui le reſſembloit ſi bien, que tous les autres iol-
dats, prins argument de telle ſimilitude, appeloyent ce
ieune homme ſouuentesfois le Prince, auquel comme
dans vn miroir, le Duc ſe delectoit ſouuent voir ſon ima
ge, ſes geſtes, & contenances: recognoiſtre ſa voix, & ſe
contempler ſoy-meſmes. En meſmes temps & pays, ce
Duc Sforce auoit vn plaiſanteur, nõmé Marcheſin, qu'il
appeloit le ſeigneur Sigiſmond Malareſte ſon fils, pour
ce qu'ils eſtoyent entierement ſemblables. De quoy ice-
luy Malateſte auoit ſi grand honte, que quand il vouloit
aller à Milan voir le Duc, ſon beau pere, il l'enuoyoit
premierement ſupplier, de mander ailleurs Marcheſin.
{h} Des ſimilitudes qui ont eſté cauſe de pluſieurs impoſtu
res, factions grandes, & entrepriſes memorables, nous
en parlerons plus commodément ci bas en quelque lieu
s'il plaiſt au Seigneur, Mais icy peut eſtre que quel-
qu'vn voudra recercher, & entendre la cauſe; pour la-
quelle on voit ſouuent les hommes procréez de diuers
parens, & en diuers lointains lieux, neantmoins ſe rap-
porter ſi bien, & proprement des traicts du viſage, & de
la compoſition du corps, que facilemeut ne ſe peuuent
diſcerner les vns des autres. Auquel ie diray premiere-
ment, qu'il faut auec l'honneur, & la reuerence qu'il ap-
partient, rapporter la ſource, & la cauſe de tels faicts, à
l'entendement de ce grand ouurier de nature (qui eſt le
Dieu tout puiſſant) lequel ne s'aſſeruiſt aux races, ni aux
pays, ny aux affections des perſonnes, mais par ſon infi-
nie & incomprehenſible prouidence, ſecrets, hauts & in-
ſcrutables iugemens, proiette ſes idées, & forme ſes crea-
tures, cõme il luy ſemble: toutesfois, voit on aduenir le
plus ſouuent, que les ſemblances des hommes, paſſent
iuſqu'aux races: & que tout animal, non ſeulement pro-
crée ſon ſemblable: mais encor luy depart ſes propres, &
naturelles vertus.
Mũſter au
liure ij. de la
coſmographie
vniuerſelle,
